title: Deploy containers to Azure Container Apps

questions.q: An embedding service must be callable by the AI API in the same environment, but not from the internet. Which ingress setting should it use?

options.text: No ingress, plus a public IP address
options.why: Learn uses ingress settings, not public IPs, to control reachability.
External ingress exposes the app to callers outside the environment.
private-link isn't one of the ingress values Learn describes.
Correct. Internal ingress makes the service reachable only within the environment.

questions.hint: Callers inside the environment need it, and the internet mustn't reach it. Which ingress mode keeps traffic inside?
questions.explain: Use external ingress for public-facing APIs and internal ingress for services called only by other services in the environment.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. You're planning environments for an AI solution with an API, a background processor, and dev, test and production stages.

rows.text: Putting the API and the background processor in the same environment lets them share networking and logging integration.
rows.why: Related services are often grouped in one environment for shared networking and logging.

rows.text: Learn recommends one shared environment for dev, test and production to keep things simple.
rows.why: Learn recommends separate environments by lifecycle to reduce blast radius.

rows.text: An environment is only a folder for resources and doesn't affect traffic between apps.
rows.why: An environment influences internal traffic, logging connections and governance.

questions.hint: Think about what an environment shares and why you'd separate lifecycle stages.
questions.explain: Environments are an isolation and management model: group related services, separate lifecycles.

questions.q: Several apps will share one environment, and the platform team wants control over its name and lifecycle. Which approach fits best?

options.text: Deploy each app with --ingress internal so they end up in one environment
options.why: Ingress controls reachability, not which environment is created.

options.text: Let az containerapp up create a new environment for each app as it deploys
options.why: containerapp up is fastest, but it makes the naming and lifecycle decisions for you.

options.text: Create the environment first with az containerapp env create, then deploy the apps into it
options.why: Correct. Creating the environment explicitly gives more control when multiple apps share it.

options.text: Create a separate resource group per app; the environment follows from that
options.why: Resource groups don't define a Container Apps environment.

questions.hint: Several apps share the environment, and you want control over its name. Should a deploy command create it implicitly?
questions.explain: Creating the environment first gives you control over naming and lifecycle, which helps when multiple apps share it.

questions.q: An AI API calls a private embedding processor, and the team validates new revisions in dev and test before production. Which environment layout follows Learn's guidance?

options.text: Per-stage environments, each holding both services, with internal ingress on the processor
options.why: Correct. Separate environments per lifecycle stage reduce blast radius, and services that talk privately belong in the same environment with internal ingress.

options.text: One environment per stage, with the processor deployed outside Container Apps as a VM
options.why: Nothing in the scenario needs a VM. Both services fit in the same environment.

options.text: One shared environment for all three stages, with the processor's ingress set to external
options.why: A shared environment removes the isolation between stages, and external ingress exposes a service that should stay private.

options.text: One environment for every app, so that the API and the processor never share networking
options.why: Splitting the API and processor apart breaks the simple private communication that a shared environment gives them.

questions.hint: Two guidelines apply: separate by lifecycle, and keep services that talk privately together.
questions.explain: Learn recommends separate environments for development, test and production, and placing services that must communicate privately in the same environment with internal ingress.

questions.q: A new revision of your AI API fails at startup, and you want to query its container logs and the platform's system logs together, in one place. What does a Container Apps environment commonly integrate with for this?

options.why: Pipeline history shows deployments you ran, not the app's runtime logs.
Registry webhooks notify about image pushes. They don't collect logs.
Correct. An environment commonly integrates with Azure Monitor logs, so you can query container and system logs in one place.
Key Vault holds secrets. It isn't where Container Apps logs go.

questions.hint: You want one queryable store for logs. Which Azure monitoring service holds logs?
questions.explain: A Container Apps environment commonly integrates with Azure Monitor logs, so you can query container logs and system logs in one place.

questions.q: Which command is the fastest way to deploy a first version of a container app, creating the environment if needed?

options.why: Correct. up can create the environment and supporting resources and returns the FQDN.
update changes an existing app.
env create only creates the environment, not the app.
create is the more explicit option and expects an existing environment.

questions.hint: One command can create the environment and the app together. It's the quickest path to a first deployment.
questions.explain: az containerapp up is the fastest initial deployment; az containerapp create is the more explicit path.

questions.q: You run `az containerapp update --yaml ./containerapp.yml --image myregistry.azurecr.io/ai-api:v3`, but the app keeps the image named in the YAML file. Why?

options.text: The YAML file is applied first and then overwritten by the flag
options.why: It's the other way round: the flag is ignored entirely.

options.text: Image changes need az containerapp up instead of update
options.why: update can change images; the issue is the --yaml behavior.

options.text: When --yaml is used, other flags are ignored
options.why: Correct. The YAML becomes the source of truth, so --image is ignored.

options.text: The registry has to be set again before each image change
options.why: Registry configuration isn't required again for each update.

questions.hint: The command used a YAML file and a flag. Which one does Container Apps treat as the source of truth?
questions.explain: With --yaml, the YAML file is the full configuration source and other flags are ignored.

questions.q: You're preparing a new machine to deploy Container Apps from the CLI. Put the steps in the order Learn's quickstart uses.
questions.hint: Sign in, update the CLI, add the extension, then register the provider.
questions.explain: Sign in, update the CLI, add or upgrade the containerapp extension, then register the Microsoft.App (and Microsoft.OperationalInsights) providers.

questions.q: A deployment of `myregistry.azurecr.io/Team/AI-Api:v1` fails with what looks like an authentication error, although the credentials are correct. What should you check first?

options.text: Whether the YAML file in source control was reviewed
options.why: Code review doesn't affect the image pull.

options.text: Whether the provider Microsoft.OperationalInsights is registered
options.why: Provider registration problems don't show up as image pull auth errors.

options.text: Whether the app was created with az containerapp up or create
options.why: Both commands pull the image the same way.

options.text: Whether the repository name in the image reference is lower case
options.why: Correct. Learn warns that non-lower-case repository names cause pull failures that look like authentication errors.

questions.hint: Pull failures can look like authentication errors. Check the case of the image path.
questions.explain: Keep the repository portion of the image reference lower case to avoid misleading pull failures.

questions.q: Your first az containerapp create in a new subscription fails with a message that the subscription isn't registered to use the namespace Microsoft.OperationalInsights. What should you run?

options.why: az upgrade updates the CLI itself, and it has no namespace parameter.
Correct. The quickstart setup registers both Microsoft.App and Microsoft.OperationalInsights.
Changing log options avoids the question. The quickstart flow registers the provider.
The extension adds CLI commands. It doesn't register resource providers in the subscription.

questions.hint: The error names a resource provider. Which az command family registers providers in a subscription?
questions.explain: Before deploying, register the resource providers: az provider register --namespace Microsoft.App and --namespace Microsoft.OperationalInsights.

questions.q: You run az containerapp update --image myregistry.azurecr.io/ai-api:v2 on a running app. You want to validate the change before it takes all traffic. What does the update create?

options.text: A new environment that copies the app's settings
options.why: Updating an app doesn't create an environment. Environments are created separately.

options.text: An in-place restart of the existing replicas
options.why: Container Apps versions configuration changes as revisions rather than patching running replicas.

options.text: A new revision that represents the new configuration
options.why: Correct. Updates usually create a new revision, which lets you validate it before shifting all traffic.

options.text: A replacement app with a new FQDN for the v2 image
options.why: The app keeps its identity and FQDN. The change is versioned as a revision.

questions.hint: Container Apps versions every configuration change. What's the name for one version of an app?
questions.explain: Container Apps uses revisions to version configuration changes. An update such as a new image tag creates a new revision.

questions.q: Engineers deploy the AI API with ad-hoc CLI flags, and test and production configurations keep drifting apart. The team wants every change reviewed. What does Learn recommend?

options.text: Use az containerapp up for every deployment so that defaults stay the same
options.why: az containerapp up is for fast first deployments. It doesn't create a reviewable record of configuration.

options.text: Make changes in the Azure portal so that the activity log records them
options.why: Portal changes are for one-off work. They aren't reviewed before they're applied.

options.text: Keep containerapp.yml in source control and apply it with --yaml after code review
options.why: Correct. YAML in source control makes deployments repeatable and reviewable and reduces drift.

options.text: Combine --yaml with extra CLI flags for the values that differ per stage
options.why: With --yaml, other flags are ignored, so the per-stage flags would silently do nothing.

questions.hint: You want a file that can go through code review and be applied the same way every time.
questions.explain: Store the YAML file in source control and apply changes through code review. With --yaml, the YAML becomes the source of truth and other flags are ignored.

questions.q: The AI API needs the embeddings API key as the variable EMBEDDINGS_API_KEY, and the key is already stored as the secret embeddings-api-key. What value should the variable have?

options.why: Correct. secretref:<secret-name> maps the secret to the variable without exposing its value.
That isn't Container Apps syntax.
Pasting the value exposes it in shell history and config.
That isn't the Container Apps reference syntax.

questions.hint: Environment variables can point to a secret by name with a special prefix.
questions.explain: Set the variable to secretref:<secret-name> (secretRef in YAML).

questions.q: You need to change LOG_LEVEL to debug on a running app without removing its other environment variables. Which command should you use?

options.why: Correct. --set-env-vars adds or updates variables without removing existing ones.
registry set configures image pull authentication.
create is for new apps.
A log level isn't sensitive and doesn't belong in secrets.

questions.hint: One flag replaces the variable list and the other adds or updates. Which keeps existing variables?
questions.explain: Use --env-vars on create and --set-env-vars on update for non-sensitive settings.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. A team stores `containerapp.yml` in Git and uses secrets for provider API keys.

rows.text: The YAML file in Git should contain the API key values so deployments are complete.
rows.why: Keep secret values out of YAML; store only secret names.

rows.text: Rotating a Container Apps secret requires rebuilding the container image.
rows.why: Secrets let you rotate values without rebuilding or redeploying the image.

rows.text: A Key Vault reference lets the app fetch a secret whose system of record is Key Vault.
rows.why: The CLI supports a Key Vault reference format for secrets.

rows.text: After a registry change, deploying a new revision and checking it starts validates the change.
rows.why: Learn recommends validating auth during rollout this way.

questions.hint: Secrets stay out of Git and images. Key Vault can be the system of record.
questions.explain: Secrets stay out of YAML and images; Key Vault can be the system of record; validate registry changes with a new revision.

questions.q: Your containerapp.yml is stored in Git. EMBEDDINGS_API_KEY must come from the Container Apps secret embeddings-api-key. How should the env entry for the ai-api container look?

options.text: name: EMBEDDINGS_API_KEY, with value: set to the key copied from the provider
options.why: That puts the secret value in Git, which the guidance says to avoid.

options.text: name: EMBEDDINGS_API_KEY, with valueFrom: secretKeyRef: embeddings-api-key
options.why: That's Kubernetes Pod syntax. Container Apps YAML uses secretRef.
Container Apps doesn't expand shell-style placeholders in YAML values.
Correct. In YAML, secretRef names the secret, so only the secret's name is stored in source control.

questions.hint: In the CLI you write secretref: in the value. YAML has its own field for the same thing.
questions.explain: In YAML, an env entry uses secretRef: <secret-name>. In the CLI, you set the value to secretref:<secret-name>. Either way, only the secret's name is stored.

questions.q: Twenty container apps pull images from one ACR registry, and rotating the registry password across all of them is costly. Which two steps follow Learn's guidance? (Select two.)

options.text: Omit credentials so the CLI infers them in production
options.why: Learn says to prefer an explicit authentication method in production.

options.text: Grant each app's identity only the AcrPull role
options.why: Correct. Grant least privilege: only AcrPull for identities that pull images.

options.text: Run az containerapp registry set with --identity system
options.why: Correct. Managed identity avoids storing long-lived registry credentials.

options.text: Grant each app's identity the Owner role on the registry
options.why: Owner is far more than pulling needs; Learn says least privilege.

questions.hint: Learn's advice for many apps pulling from ACR is to avoid long-lived credentials and grant least privilege.
questions.explain: Prefer managed identity for ACR and assign only AcrPull.

questions.q: A vendor's model image is in a third-party private registry that doesn't support Azure managed identities. How should you configure the container app to pull it?

options.text: az containerapp registry set with --server, --username and --password
options.why: Correct. Username and password works with registries that don't support Azure-managed identities.

options.text: Grant the app's managed identity the AcrPull role on the vendor's registry
options.why: AcrPull is an Azure Container Registry role. It can't be assigned on a third-party registry.

options.text: Store the vendor password in an environment variable named REGISTRY_PASSWORD
options.why: Container Apps doesn't read registry credentials from app environment variables.

options.text: az containerapp registry set with --server and --identity system
options.why: Managed identity pulls need a registry that accepts Azure identities, such as ACR.

questions.hint: Managed identity isn't an option for this registry. What's the simplest credential type that works with any registry?
questions.explain: Container Apps supports registry authentication with username and password, and with managed identity when the registry is ACR. For registries without Azure-managed identity support, use username and password.

questions.q: The same app is deployed to dev, test and prod, and you suspect a different registry is configured in one of them. Which command shows the registries configured on an app?

options.why: Correct. It lists the registries configured on the app, which helps you spot drift between environments.
This lists revisions and their state, not registry configuration.
This shows the environment. Registry settings belong to each app.
This lists repositories inside a registry. It doesn't show which registries an app is set up to use.

questions.hint: Registry configuration belongs to the app. Look for the registry sub-command of az containerapp.
questions.explain: Use az containerapp registry list (or show --server) to confirm which registries an app is configured to use, for example to detect drift across environments.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. You're switching a production container app to pull from ACR with managed identity.

rows.text: The app's identity should get the AcrPush role so that future CI changes don't need new role assignments.
rows.why: Grant least privilege: an identity that only pulls images needs only AcrPull.

rows.text: Image references should use fully qualified names that include the registry hostname.
rows.why: Fully qualified names avoid ambiguity about which registry an image comes from.

rows.text: Because the CLI can sometimes infer ACR credentials, production scripts can safely leave authentication out.
rows.why: Learn says to prefer an explicit authentication approach in production so behavior is predictable.

rows.text: You should deploy a new revision and confirm it starts before assuming the registry change works.
rows.why: Validating auth during rollout catches pull failures before you rely on the change.

questions.hint: Think least privilege, unambiguous image names, explicit auth, and proving the change with a real revision.
questions.explain: Best practices: prefer managed identity for ACR, grant only AcrPull, use fully qualified image names, and validate the change by deploying a new revision and checking that it starts.

questions.q: Match each verification need to the command.

items.text: See whether any instances of the revision are running
items.why: Replicas are the running instances of a revision.

questions.hint: System logs, all revisions, and running instances each have their own command.
questions.explain: Logs explain errors, revisions show versions, replicas show what's running.

questions.q: After an update, users still get the old behavior. You want to confirm that the update created a new revision and that it became healthy. Which command should you run?

options.why: registry list shows pull configuration only.
Correct. Listing revisions confirms a new revision exists and becomes active.
env show describes the environment, not app revisions.
secret list doesn't show revision state.

questions.hint: You want to see whether the update produced a new version and whether it's healthy.
questions.explain: Use revisions for rollout validation: list them after updates.

questions.q: For each statement, select Yes if the statement is true. Otherwise, select No. You're investigating a startup failure of a new AI API revision.

rows.text: az containerapp logs show is a good first step to capture startup errors.
rows.why: Learn says to start with logs.

rows.text: By default, az containerapp logs show streams every line ever written by the app.
rows.why: By default it returns a limited number of lines; use --follow and --tail to stream.

rows.text: If replica list shows zero replicas, the revision has crashed.
rows.why: Zero replicas can also mean the app scaled to zero.

questions.hint: Logs are the first step. Think about how many lines logs show returns by default, and what zero replicas can mean.
questions.explain: Start with logs; replicas help detect scale-to-zero, crash loops or missing traffic.

questions.q: A web client can't reach your newly deployed AI API. Before reading any logs, you want to confirm the ingress settings and get the FQDN. Which command should you run?

options.why: Correct. It shows the app's configuration, including ingress, so you can spot internal-vs-external mistakes and get the FQDN.
System logs help with platform issues, but they don't show the app's ingress configuration.
The environment doesn't hold each app's ingress settings or FQDN.
Replicas tell you whether instances are running, not how ingress is configured.

questions.hint: You want the app's own configuration, not its logs or instances.
questions.explain: Before diving into logs, confirm app configuration and ingress with az containerapp show. It catches mistakes such as internal ingress where you expected external, and it returns the FQDN.

questions.q: While you send test traffic to the AI API, you want to watch new log lines as they arrive, with more history than the default. Which command fits?

options.why: This switches to platform logs. It doesn't follow new output.
This lists revisions, including inactive ones. It doesn't show logs.
Correct. --follow streams logs in real time, and --tail raises the number of lines returned.
This lists running instances. It doesn't stream their output.

questions.hint: You need two options: one keeps the stream open, and one sets how many lines come back.
questions.explain: az containerapp logs show returns a limited number of lines by default. Add --follow to tail in real time and --tail to increase the count.
